items.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: that he went to Handy — W.C. Handy’s music store there in Nashville, Tennessee.

ctx.x: Well it’s kind of tragic in a way. See my mother and father, they’re from Birmingham, Alabama. And my grandparents on his side, they own land, and they worked the land, and also from what I understand they would provide seed and fertilizer, and then the neighbors, they would all sharecrop and then they’d split the proceeds. And my dad, let’s see I had three aunts and two uncles, and so my dad, they sent him to an industrial school in Tennessee, which later I guess became part of the school system, the college…

that he went to Handy — W.C. Handy’s music store there in Nashville, Tennessee. Now my dad was born what, in the 1890s, so that had to be what, the early 1900s. He used to tell me that story. And my dad played ukulele and he sang and he would sing “Waiting for Ships that Never Come In” and they would do the recitations. Oh yeah. That’s when people would visit. Because the big thing then was visiting in various homes and entertaining. And my mother — on my father’s side my grandfather was a preacher. He was…

on the radio with a singing group and he had a bit of a name, so they got Saunders to front the band. And so anyhow I’d go by and watch the rehearsals and I’d watch the drummer, Maxey, Norville Maxey was the drummer. I’d watch him to see what he was doing. So then I found the name James Brown was forming a small band and he needed a drummer. Well in the meantime also, Mr. Thompson, our barber, he had been in the Cavalry I think back in the Midwest. And he’d been in the Cavalry band. So in his basement he had all…
